---
title: "How it works"
subtitle: "Deterministic statistics first, then a bounded agent loop, then a gate that removes claims it cannot verify."
---

## The shape of it

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  subgraph replay["Replay, so a result is reproducible"]
    BUNDLE["Incident bundle<br/><small>Parquet, read through DuckDB</small>"]
  end

  subgraph deterministic["Deterministic, no model"]
    ANOM["Robust anomaly scores<br/><small>median and MAD</small>"]
    RANK["Personalised PageRank<br/><small>over the service graph</small>"]
    ABST{"Above the<br/>abstention<br/>threshold?"}
  end

  subgraph agent["Agent loop, budgeted"]
    CMD["Commander<br/><small>picks the next hypothesis</small>"]
    SPEC["4 specialists<br/><small>metrics, logs, traces, change</small>"]
    BOARD["Hypothesis board"]
    CRIT["Critic<br/><small>argues against the leader</small>"]
    REP["Reporter"]
  end

  subgraph verify["Verification"]
    GATE["Exit gate<br/><small>6 checks</small>"]
  end

  BUNDLE --> ANOM --> RANK --> ABST
  ABST -->|no| OUT2["Abstain, naming the<br/>threshold it failed"]
  ABST -->|yes| CMD
  CMD --> SPEC --> BOARD --> CRIT
  CRIT -->|"more to test"| CMD
  CRIT -->|"settled"| REP --> GATE
  GATE -->|"claims survive"| OUT1["Report, every claim cited"]
  GATE -->|"support too thin"| OUT2
```

## Why the statistics come first

Two reasons, and the second is the one that matters.

**Cost.** A model that reads forty services to find one is forty times the tokens of a model
that reads three.

**A floor you can compare against.** `b0` is the deterministic triage alone, with no model at
all. It is the baseline every agent configuration must beat. A multi-agent system that cannot
beat a page of statistics is a multi-agent system that should not exist, and the comparison is
reported whichever way it comes out.

::: {.callout-note}
## Median and MAD, not mean and standard deviation

A fault is a spike. A spike moves a mean, and it inflates a standard deviation, so the
z-score of the spike against statistics that include the spike is smaller than it should be.
Median and median absolute deviation are barely moved by it, so the anomaly stays visible.
:::

## Why PageRank over the service graph

The service that looks worst is usually downstream of the one that broke. If payment starts
failing, the frontend's error rate goes up too, and the frontend is louder because it takes
every request.

Personalised PageRank walks the call graph from the anomalous services and asks which service
best *explains* the pattern, rather than which one shows it most.

::: {.callout-important}
## And on real recordings it does not work yet

On the eight recordings available, the ranking blames `frontend` for all three payment
failures. That is the symptom over the cause, which is the exact thing this mechanism exists to
prevent. It is the second largest open problem in the project, recorded in the phase reports
with the evidence.
:::

## The four roles, and what each cannot do

The constraints are more interesting than the capabilities.

| Role | Does | **Cannot** | Why the limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commander | Chooses the next hypothesis and which specialist tests it | Call an evidence tool | Separates deciding what to look at from looking |
| Specialists | Gather evidence on one hypothesis, one question each | See each other's answers | Four independent looks, not one conversation converging on the first guess |
| Critic | Argues against the leading hypothesis | Gather new evidence | It cannot build its own case, only test the one on the table |
| Reporter | Writes claims, each naming its evidence | Cite a record no tool produced | The gate re-runs every citation, so an invented one fails |

## Typed tools, not free-form queries

A model never writes a query. It picks a tool and supplies validated arguments; the tool builds
the query.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  M["Model picks a tool<br/>and supplies arguments"] --> V["Pydantic model<br/><small>extra=forbid</small>"]
  V --> Q["Tool builds the query"]
  Q --> B[("Backend<br/><small>Prometheus, Jaeger,<br/>OpenSearch, or the bundle</small>")]
  B --> C["Cap applied"]
  C --> E["Evidence record<br/><small>query, window, backend fingerprint,<br/>row hash, arguments to re-run it</small>"]
  E --> ID["ev_&lt;kind&gt;_&lt;sha256[:12]&gt;"]
```

This buys three things:

1. **A query nobody can inject into.** The realistic attack here is a log line, not a prompt.
2. **A cap on every call**, so one tool cannot fill a context window.
3. **An evidence id that is a hash of what was asked and what came back**, which is what makes
   re-execution meaningful.

## The exit gate

Six checks on the finished report. A claim that fails one is removed.

| Check | Refuses |
|---|---|
| `coverage` | A claim citing an evidence id nothing recorded |
| `re_execution` | A citation that does not re-run to the same hash |
| `numbers` | A number in prose that its cited evidence does not contain |
| `consistency` | A report that disagrees with the notebook or the timeline |
| `confidence_sanity` | A confidence the evidence does not support |
| `abstention` | Naming a service whose support is below the threshold |

::: {.callout-warning}
## What the gate cannot check

Whether a claim says anything.

All forty claims across the ten showcase reports are true, cited, re-runnable, and
uninformative: four of five describe the investigation rather than the incident. Six checks ask
whether a claim is **supported**; none asks whether it is **informative**, and a report of
supported tautologies passes cleanly.

The cause is the deterministic stub rather than the system. It still means the only end-to-end
exercise of the gate that CI runs is one where the numbers check verifies zero numbers. Whether
to add a seventh check is an open question rather than a change made quietly.
:::

## Keeping the answer away from the agent

The benchmark is worthless if the agent can see the label. That is not something to be careful
about; it is made mechanically impossible.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  L[("Labels<br/><small>separate package</small>")] -.->|"import forbidden,<br/>enforced by a graph walk"| A["Agent packages"]
  L --> EV["Eval code only"]
  CAN["Random canary<br/>in every label"] --> SCAN["Every prompt scanned"]
  FLAG["Fault flag flips"] -.->|"excluded"| CHG["Change log the agent reads"]
  style L fill:#fff8e8,stroke:#e6cf9a
```

Six controls, of which these are the load-bearing ones:

- Labels live outside the bundles, in a package only the eval code may import, enforced by a
  test that **walks the import graph** rather than grepping, so an alias cannot hide.
- Each label carries a random canary string, and every prompt is scanned for it.
- The change log the agent reads excludes fault flag flips, because otherwise the answer is in
  the evidence.
- Memory is writable on train scenarios only, since a memory of "payment failed like this last
  time" is ground truth wearing a different hat.

That import-graph test has caught two real routes during development. Neither was a leak;
both were routes a leak could later travel.
